# Blob uploaders: a write-only credential for the blob bucket

Published from the repository note platform/docs/blob-uploader.md, measured on 2026-09-21. The short version for agents is on the agents page (https://lakehousebox.com/agents#relay); the routes are in the API reference (https://lakehousebox.com/docs/api/), the commands in the CLI reference (https://lakehousebox.com/docs/cli/).

The founder's item 1 of 2026-09-21 (platform/STATE.md, 03:40 UTC): a scoped, long-lived, revocable credential that can only drop files into a catalog's blob bucket <handle>--<catalog>--blobs (b-<uuid> on catalogs created before 2026-09-20; the API's bucket field and the recipe's blob_bucket spell it, this document writes <blobs> for it). For a relay, a camera, a field device, a partner that sends you files, a CI job that publishes artefacts: anything that must write and must never read, list what others wrote, or come near the tables and the catalog.

```
lhbox catalog uploader create garden --name camera-north --prefix photos/north/ --save ~/camera-north.json
lhbox catalog uploader list   garden
lhbox catalog uploader revoke garden --uploader camera-north
```

lhbox connect says so in its notes (uploaders_note in GET /v1/connection): the catalog's own credential is for engines and for you, never for a device.

The file bucket takes data file types (photos, documents, archives and data formats; since 2026-10-02): an upload of another type is refused with 415 UnsupportedFileType. The list is on File types.

## What the credential is, exactly

One IAM identity in the store, u-<warehouse_uuid>-<8 hex of the uploader id>, granted its rights by two statements in the blob bucket's plain bucket policy (an S3 write, PutBucketPolicy; since 2026-09-21, PLAN.md item 11 -- before that the same two statements were an inline user policy, PutUserPolicy, name uploader, an IAM write of 10 s at the host's identity count; uploaders from before keep theirs, uploader.grant_mode NULL). The control plane writes them once and never re-puts them:

```
{"Sid": "tm-up-<identity>-put", "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": {"AWS": ["arn:aws:iam::*:user/u-<uuid>-<short>"]},
 "Action": ["s3:PutObject"], "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::<blobs>/photos/north/*"]}
{"Sid": "tm-up-<identity>-list", "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": {"AWS": ["arn:aws:iam::*:user/u-<uuid>-<short>"]},   <- only with list: true
 "Action": ["s3:ListBucket"], "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::<blobs>"],
 "Condition": {"StringLike": {"s3:prefix": ["photos/north/*"]}}}
```

The statements sit next to the tenant's own data-path statement and the lifecycle grant in the same document (docs/permissions-and-access.md, "How identities and policies are laid out"); a revocation removes exactly the two Sids and nothing else.

| the holder can | the holder cannot |
|---|---|
| PutObject under the prefix, single or multipart (create, part, complete, abort) | read, HEAD, delete or overwrite-then-read anything, including its own uploads |
| with list: true: ListObjectsV2 with ?prefix=<its prefix or deeper> | list without a prefix, or another prefix |
|  | anything on the table bucket <handle>--<catalog> (no statement names it) |
|  | use the catalog: POST /v1/oauth/tokens mints a token for any valid pair, and the table-bucket policy, which names only t-<uuid> and t-<uuid>-ro, refuses it |

No prefix (prefix: "") means the whole blob bucket except its _ area for every object action (a whole-bucket lister with list: true still SEES the key names there: the listing is checked on the bucket, not on keys) (_sink/, _index/, _lhbox/, the service's own: a write under _sink/ became rows of a table, review 2026-09-24). One explicit Deny per blob bucket (<blobs>/_* for every u-<catalog>-* identity, and since 2026-09-28 the key <blobs>/AGENTS.md too: the catalog's instructions for agents are its writers', never a drop box's) says it; in the store an explicit bucket-policy Deny beats every Allow, the identity's own policy included, so uploaders created before the change are covered too (the Deny is written on those buckets at the next start). A new uploader's prefix may not start with _; list: true without a prefix lists the whole blob bucket (no Condition), and the answer's scope says which. A prefix without a trailing slash confines to keys that start with it: photos covers photos.jpg and photos/a.jpg both. The prefix grammar is what S3 keys allow minus what the policy engine would read as a pattern: letters, digits, . _ - / = @ :; no leading slash, no empty or dot segments, no * ? $.

expires_at is recorded and shown (status: expired after it); the key itself stays valid until revoked. Revocation is the only thing that stops a holder today.

## The IAM cost, stated

Every IAM write costs the store a propagation deadline (10 s at the host's identity count on 2026-09-20, about 0.1–0.3 s after the fixture purge / patch #4; STATE.md 21:10 UTC). Designed for the fewest writes:

| operation | IAM writes | which |
|---|---|---|
| create an uploader | 2 (was 3 until 2026-09-21) | CreateUser, CreateAccessKey, then the two statements merged into the blob bucket's policy -- an S3 call, no propagation (in that order: the key never exists with any grant but the final one; an identity with neither actions nor policies is denied everything) |
| list | 0 |  |
| any later call, GET /v1/connection included | 0 | the statements are never re-put |
| revoke | 2 (3 for an uploader from before) | DeleteAccessKey first (that is the revocation; the key is refused from then on), then the statements off the bucket policy (S3) and DeleteUser; an uploader with an inline policy (grant_mode NULL) gets DeleteUserPolicy in between; before the answer, idempotent |
| delete the catalog | 2 per uploader (3 for one from before) | inside the background teardown that already carries the tenant's writes; the statements go with the blob bucket; each step lands in the tombstone's storage map |

The unit tests count them through the fake's call log (control_plane/tests/test_uploaders.py). Each uploader is one more identity in the store, so make one per device or partner, not one per file.

## Consuming what was uploaded

The uploader cannot read; you do, from the catalog side, with the catalog's own credential (lhbox connect, blob_bucket and blob_example_python in GET /v1/connection):

```
-- DuckDB, with the S3 secret of the connect recipe (lhbox_s3)
SELECT filename, size, content
FROM read_blob('s3://<blobs>/photos/north/*.jpg');
-- Parquet dropped by a partner, straight into a table of the catalog
INSERT INTO garden.sensors SELECT * FROM read_parquet('s3://<blobs>/partner-acme/2026-09/*.parquet');
```

Index files in a table (the pattern of our first tenant: photos in the bucket, one row per photo in a table) and hand download links out from your side with generate_presigned_url('get_object', …); the uploader has no GetObject to presign with. Deleting or moving what was uploaded is yours too.

## Seeing what was uploaded: the Files section and two routes (added 2026-09-22)

The account page's catalog view has a Files section: the blob bucket as folders and files, with thumbnails for images (.jpg .jpeg .png .webp .gif .svg .avif), a preview on click, a download link, and Load more past 1,000 entries. It is fed by two read-level routes (and, since 2026-10-10, writes through two write-level ones: below):

```
GET /v1/warehouses/{id}/blobs?prefix=&delimiter=/&token=&max_keys=1000&urls=0     read level
GET /v1/warehouses/{id}/blobs/presign?key=<object key>&expires=900&download=0     read level
```

The same preview opens from the SQL explorer's results (added 2026-09-24): when a result has a bucket column and an object_key column (the columns an index rule writes, ingest-sink.md "index rules") and the bucket is the blob bucket of a catalog you can open, each such row gets a View cell (Open for files that are not images). The click mints one presigned GET for that object with the second route above, at read level on that catalog; nothing is fetched until you click, and a bucket that is not one of your catalogs' gets no cell.

- The listing is signed as the catalog's own identity (t-<uuid>, the pair the bucket policy names), never as the store's admin: what a holder of the connection recipe could list with boto3 is exactly what the route answers. ListObjectsV2 with prefix, a delimiter (default /; empty for a flat listing) and a continuation token, at most 1,000 entries a page (max_keys is clamped); the answer carries objects[{key, name, size, last_modified, etag}] and prefixes[{prefix, name}], truncated and next_token. _sink/ (the sink's transit prefix, ingest-sink.md) shows as a folder like any other. A catalog from before blob buckets gets its bucket on the first look and lists empty.

- File bytes never pass through the control plane. ?urls=1 adds to every object a presigned GET URL (AWS SigV4 query auth, signed with the catalog's own pair, 900 s) on the store's public endpoint, path-style (https://s3.<host>/<bucket>/<key>?X-Amz-Algorithm=…&X-Amz-Expires=900&X-Amz-Signature=…); the page puts them in <img src loading=lazy>, which needs no CORS, only the site CSP's img-src naming the store (the gateway's Caddyfile.prod). /blobs/presign mints one URL for one key; with download=1 the signed query also carries response-content-disposition=attachment; filename=…, which the store copies onto its answer so the browser saves the file under its name without leaving the page (a cross-origin download attribute is ignored; the header is what works). Expiry 30–3600 s, clamped; the key is not checked for existence (the store answers 404 to whoever follows the link). Presigning is arithmetic: one store call per page, none per URL.

- Who may look: the caller's read grant on the catalog (docs/permissions-and-access.md); an organisation human without one is 403 forbidden naming who can grant, a stranger and an agent without a grant 404 warehouse_not_found, like every other /v1/warehouses/{id}/… route. An uploader's S3 pair is not an API credential (401), and the store refuses its own ListObjectsV2 and GetObject anyway (the matrix below): the view exists because the catalog's identity can read what the uploader could only write.

Not yet measured on the live store: a presigned GET through the gateway at s3.lakehousebox.com (Caddy forwards Host unchanged and signs nothing, so the same reasoning as for header-signed requests applies); the first live click on a thumbnail is that measurement and belongs in platform/STATE.md. The unit suite (control_plane/tests/test_files_view.py) recomputes every minted signature with a stdlib SigV4 independent of botocore.

### Uploading, new folders and deleting from the Files section (added 2026-10-10)

The founder asked for what an S3 console does: Upload (a button, or files dropped anywhere on the page while the Files section is shown), New folder, and Delete on a file's row and in its preview. Write level on the catalog; a reader sees none of it. Two routes:

```
POST   /v1/warehouses/{id}/blobs/upload   {"key": "photos/a.jpg", "content_type": "image/jpeg"}   write level
DELETE /v1/warehouses/{id}/blobs?key=<object key>                                             write level
```

- The bytes still never pass through the API. /blobs/upload answers one presigned PUT (SigV4 query auth, the catalog's own pair, 900 s, path-style on the store's public endpoint) bound to the key, the PUT method and, when given, the Content-Type (a signed header: the browser must send exactly it; measured on a local store: the signed type 200, another 403). The page PUTs each file with progress, three at a time, and asks before replacing a file of the same name (S3 overwrites silently).

- What the store enforces applies unchanged, because the PUT is made with the catalog's pair through the public gateway: the bucket's storage quota (the organisation's allowance) and the file-type gate (research/53 §3, 415 UnsupportedFileType). The page words both (files_rules.js uploadErrorText).

- New folder is a folder marker: the key ending in / with an empty body (the gate accepts it). The listing hides a folder's own marker from its contents, and the store keeps one after a folder's last file goes. An empty folder is deleted from inside it ("Delete this empty folder": its marker, one key). A folder dragged onto the page is not uploaded (the browser hands over no readable file for it); the page says so.

- Delete is one key, as the catalog's identity, never a prefix; idempotent; after the page's own confirm.

- The platform's places are refused by both routes and by the page before it asks: the service area, every root key starting with _ (_sink/ feed intake, _index/ index state, _lhbox/ probe files, and any later one: the uploaders' deny statement's own rule), and the root AGENTS.md (its own audited route with a lost-update guard). The page offers no upload inside them.

- Replacing is asked about before the upload, also for a name past the 1,000 keys the listing loaded (one exact listing per such file).

- Both are audited: catalog.blob_upload_url (the key; the PUT itself is the store's) and catalog.blob_delete.

- An MCP access token needs catalogs:write for either (every mutation under /v1/warehouses/).

### Finding and using files (added 2026-10-10)

No new route: the page does all of it with the routes above.

- Folders upload too: dropped on the page (the browser's directory entries are walked, webkitGetAsEntry then readEntries in batches, as the S3 and GCS consoles do) or chosen with Upload folder (webkitdirectory). Each file keeps its path under the folder's own name. A running total and Cancel sit on top of the uploads.

- Filter by name and sort (name, size, date) over the entries loaded; with more than 1,000 entries the filter looks only at those loaded, and says so.

- Select several files: copy their paths or s3:// URIs, or delete them after one confirm.

- A row's ⋯ menu: Copy path, Copy S3 URI, Copy download link (a presigned GET valid one hour, the route's maximum; anyone holding it can fetch the file until then), Delete. For a CSV, Parquet or JSON file also Query in SQL (a temporary view file_<name> over a link signed for an hour, read by DuckDB in the tab; nothing is copied, Save as table keeps it) and Make a table… (the Import dialog with that link as its source).

- Parquet previews: the schema, the row count and the first 20 rows, read by DuckDB in the tab.

## Prefix design

- One prefix per device or partner (photos/north/, partner-acme/), so revoking one revokes one.

- Put the date in the key, not in the prefix, unless you want the credential to expire with the month (--prefix drops/2026-09/ is a cheap time box).

- A prefix that engines can glob: read_parquet('s3://<blobs>/partner-acme/*/*.parquet').

- The blob bucket counts against the catalog's storage tier like the table bucket does (/v1/usage).

- A public folder is world-readable. When the catalog is public and its admin published a folder of this bucket (lhbox catalog publish <name> --confirm --files public/, docs/public-warehouses.md, "Public files"), every file under that folder can be read and listed by anyone with no credentials, from the moment it lands. An uploader whose prefix is inside the public folder publishes what it drops; keep device prefixes outside it unless that is the point. Uploader and tenant writes are unaffected by publishing (measured, Q8).

## Expiring what uploaders drop: lifecycle rules (added 2026-09-21)

The catalog credential at write level can put S3 lifecycle rules on the blob bucket — expire camera/ after 90 days, abort multipart uploads not completed in 7 days — and they apply to everything under the prefix, what uploaders wrote included. The uploader itself cannot set or read them (measured 403 on ?lifecycle while its PutObject was 200), nor can the read-only identity. lhbox catalog lifecycle set <catalog> --prefix photos/north/ --expire-days 90; the API, the boto3 form, when deletion happens (up to 24 h after an object is due) and why table buckets never carry rules: https://lakehousebox.com/docs/lifecycle/.

## The drop box: FTP, FTPS and SFTP for devices that speak nothing else

Running since 2026-09-24 at ftp.lakehousebox.com, on its own host (al-dropbox1), separate from the one that holds the data; the first user is a garden camera that has uploaded a photo every few minutes since then. --protocols ftps,sftp (or ftp) on lhbox catalog uploader create gives the uploader a generated drop-box login (<organisation>.<catalog>.<uploader>) and password, shown once like the secret; the answer's dropbox block names the host, the ports (FTP and FTPS on 21 with passive ports 50000-50019, SFTP on 2222) and status: ready (a deployment without a drop box says not_deployed there, and the uploader's S3 key works either way). Design and measurements: research/32-device-intake.md §4.

A device logs in with that login and uploads into any folder; each finished file is written into the blob bucket under the uploader's prefix as the uploader (so the store still confines it to the prefix and it still cannot read anything), within seconds. The drop box is write-only: it lists nothing already uploaded. FTPS is explicit TLS with a certificate for ftp.lakehousebox.com. Plain FTP is offered for devices without TLS: the password and the files then cross the network unencrypted, and choosing it is the customer's call. How many drop-box uploaders an organisation may have is a limit of its plan (dropbox_uploaders, 10 by default; FTP, FTPS and SFTP are options of the same feature). Revoking the uploader refuses the next login at once, and so does its expires_at once passed.

Limits: a file of at most 256 MiB; password login only (the generated 24-character password; SSH keys are not accepted); passive FTP only (active mode is off); and while more than 1 GiB of one uploader's files waits to be relayed (the organisation over its storage quota, say), that uploader's next login is refused until the relay catches up. To turn uploads into rows of a table, add an index rule (docs/ingest-sink.md, "Files that become rows").

## Revocation and rotation

DELETE /v1/warehouses/{id}/uploaders/{id|name}: the key is deleted at the store before anything else, so a request signed with it is refused at once and a multipart upload in flight cannot complete. There is no rotate: a lost or leaked secret is revoke + create (the name is free again; 4 IAM writes in all, 6 before 2026-09-21). Deleting the catalog removes every uploader identity with it. uploader.create and uploader.revoke are audited (name, prefix, list, identity, key id, the writes; never the secret).

## Routes

```
POST   /v1/warehouses/{id}/uploaders                 {name, prefix?, list?, expires_at?, protocols?}   write level; 201; the secret once
GET    /v1/warehouses/{id}/uploaders?include_revoked=  read level; never a secret
DELETE /v1/warehouses/{id}/uploaders/{uploader_id|name}                                   write level; the key first
GET    /v1/warehouses/{id}/blobs?prefix=&delimiter=/&token=&max_keys=&urls=          read level; the blob bucket as the tenant (Files)
GET    /v1/warehouses/{id}/blobs/presign?key=&expires=&download=                     read level; one presigned GET URL
```

CLI: lhbox catalog uploader create|list|revoke. create refuses to run without --save FILE (0600, nothing printed) or --show-key (printed once), so no identity is ever created whose secret nobody received; with --json, --save masks the secret everywhere in the answer, recipes included.

## Live matrix, measured 2026-09-21 (real output; both runs 30 probes)

Two runs of the same matrix with a stdlib SigV4 signer (the CLI's doctor signer plus a payload hash):

- The routes, end to end, against a real store (this worktree's control plane on the laptop, talking to the local stack's store through the gateway): POST /v1/warehouses 41.4 s (the 4 tenant IAM writes), POST …/uploaders 201 in 20.6 s twice (iam_writes: [CreateUser, CreateAccessKey, PutUserPolicy]), GET …/uploaders 200 with no secret in the body, DELETE …/uploaders/{id} 200 in 30.7 s (storage: {access_key: ok, user_policy: ok, user: ok}), DELETE /v1/warehouses/{id} 202, tombstone with uploader_<short>_key|policy|user: ok for both uploaders.

- The store on al-lake1 (https://s3.lakehousebox.com, https://catalog.lakehousebox.com): the exact IAM / S3Tables calls the route makes, as the admin, from the host, with a fresh t-, two u- identities and a fresh table bucket; everything removed afterwards. The control plane build with the route was not deployed for this run (another session owns deploys; the branch is not pushed). IAM timings on the host: CreateUser 0.27 s, CreateAccessKey 10.3 s, PutUserPolicy 10.4 s, every Delete* 10.3 s (the propagation deadline of STATE 21:10 UTC), and 20–31 s per write in the second run while another writer held the IAM lock.

Status codes as answered, identical in both runs (relay = prefix photos/, lister = the same with list: true, tenant = t-<uuid>, the positive control with the same key shape):

| request | got |
|---|---|
| relay PUT b/photos/a.txt | 200 |
| relay PUT b/other/a.txt (outside the prefix) / tenant, same key | 403 / 200 |
| relay GET, HEAD, DELETE b/photos/a.txt (its own upload) / tenant GET | 403, 403, 403 / 200 |
| relay ListObjectsV2 b and b?prefix=photos/ (list: false) / tenant | 403, 403 / 200 |
| lister ListObjectsV2 b?prefix=photos/, ?prefix=photos/2026/ | 200, 200 (KeyCount 1) |
| lister ListObjectsV2 b (no prefix), ?prefix=other/ | 403, 403 |
| lister GET b/photos/a.txt (listing is not reading) | 403 |
| relay PUT w/x/y/data/a.parquet (a real 277-byte parquet), ListObjectsV2 w | 403, 403 |
| tenant PUT w/x/y/data/a.parquet (positive control, same key) | 200 |
| tenant PUT w/x/y/data/a.txt (the probe shape CLAUDE.md warns about) | 403 AccessDenied for the tenant too: a .txt proves nothing |
| relay multipart photos/big.bin: CreateMultipartUpload, UploadPart 1, CompleteMultipartUpload; Abort of a second | 200, 200, 200; 204 |
| relay CreateMultipartUpload other/big.bin (outside the prefix) | 403 |
| relay POST /v1/oauth/tokens with its pair | 200, a token is minted (the store checks the pair only) |
| relay with that token: GET /v1/config?warehouse=s3://w/ | 200: discovery answers any valid identity; it grants nothing |
| relay with that token: GET /v1/w/namespaces, POST /v1/w/namespaces / tenant | 404, 403 / 200, 200 (the table-bucket policy hides the warehouse and refuses the write) |
| relay PUT b/photos/b.txt after revoke / lister, same key | 403 / 200 |

Two observations from the runs that are not about the uploader: (a) a 4-byte PAR1 stand-in for a parquet file was answered 500 by the host's table bucket (200 by the local one), so the positive control uses a real parquet written by DuckDB; (b) DeleteTableBucket answered 409 BucketNotEmpty for 20–30 s after the last object under x/y/data/ was deleted (204), then 200: the emptiness check lags object deletion, which is also why a tombstone can record table_bucket: HTTP 409 until the startup sweep retries.
